To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
weak ties, not strong, play critical role in networks.
weak ties are better than no ties, but they are not better than strong ties.
weak ties are more associated with partnership development than are strong ties and that partners' partners are a useful source of information for identifying and developing weak ties.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between Granovetter (1973) "strength of weak ties" and partnership development.
how social network theory and research may inform the study of partnerships.
the role of social networks in the development of partnerships and the creation and appropriation social capital in leisure settings.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
weak ties are not only better than no ties but that they are better than strong ties for partnership development.
weak ties, when nurtured, are the most important network ties in the development of partnerships and in creating social capital.
the strength of weak (and strong) ties is a function of the level(s) of network analysis, and that the most productive approach is to examine the interplay of the three levels.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
weak ties are the key to partnership development.
weak ties are strong ties" and that "strong ties are weak ties."
the "strength of weak ties" is a useful concept to guide research and policy in partnership development and social capital creation in leisure contexts.
The main takeaway from our work is that
network analysis is a powerful tool that can help us better understand the processes and outcomes of partnership and social capital development.
the strength of weak (and strong) ties must be assessed at multiple levels of analysis.
leisure researchers need to be more aware of the importance of weak ties and of their potential to strengthen the ties they have already established.
